samples.summary: `revokeInvite` deletes an invite by id without scoping it to the workspace the caller owns (cross-tenant IDOR)
samples.evidence: The diff gates the revoke-invite button behind `isOwner` in the UI (workspace-settings.tsx:404) and the accompanying doc asserts "The backend authorization was already correct" (docs/tasks/active/20260809-workspace-settings-owner-gating-lessons.md:22). The enforced path does not match that claim. `WorkspaceService.revokeInvite(workspaceId, inviteId, userId)` calls `assertOwner(workspaceId, userId)` on line 138 and then executes `this.prisma.workspaceInvite.delete({ where: { id: inviteId } })` on line 139 — the `where` clause contains no `workspaceId`, so the owner check is performed against a workspace that has nothing to do with the row being deleted. Attack: user X, who is the legitimate owner of workspace A, sends `DELETE /workspaces/<A-slug>/invites/<invite-id-belonging-to-workspace-B>` (workspace.controller.ts:103-115 passes the raw path param straight through). `assertOwner` passes for A, and B's pending invite is destroyed — a cross-tenant write/denial of onboarding. Contrast `ApiKeyService.revoke(id, resolvedId)` (api-key.controller.ts:63), which does pass the workspace for scoping, showing the intended pattern. Exploitability is bounded by having to know the target invite's UUID (it is not the value in the invite link, which is `token`), so I could not complete a chain that discovers the id from outside the owning workspace — hence a missing tenant scope on a destructive operation rather than a confirmed end-to-end exploit.

samples.summary: API key listing is only member-gated on the server while the UI presents it as owner-only, so the `isOwner` gate this change follows is not backed by an enforced check
samples.evidence: This change adopts `enabled: !!workspaceId && !!isOwner` for the invites query explicitly "matching the existing api-keys query" (docs/tasks/active/20260809-workspace-settings-owner-gating-todo.md, Plan) and keeps the API Keys section behind `isOwner` (workspace-settings.tsx:425). But `GET /workspaces/:workspaceId/api-keys` calls `this.workspaceService.assertMember(resolvedId, userId)` (api-key.controller.ts:50), not `assertOwner` as the create/revoke handlers on lines 33 and 62 do. Any non-owner member can therefore curl the endpoint directly and read every key's name, prefix, scopes, createdAt and lastUsedAt for the workspace — the hidden section reads as an access control but is purely cosmetic here. Only key metadata leaks (the secret is returned once at creation), which is why this is minor rather than a credential exposure.

samples.summary: Invite tokens are unlimited-use, never consumed, and may carry `role: "owner"`, so a leaked link grants perpetual workspace ownership
samples.evidence: `acceptInvite` (workspace.service.ts:142-182) looks the invite up by token, checks only `expiresAt`, and creates the membership with `role: invite.role` (line 166); the invite row is never deleted or marked used, so the same link works for an unbounded number of distinct accounts. `CreateInviteDto` permits `role: 'owner'` (workspace.dto.ts:37-40, WORKSPACE_ROLES includes 'owner') and the frontend's `createInvite` sends no expiration (workspace-settings.tsx:111 -> api/workspaces.ts:111-122), so every invite this page creates has `expiresAt: null` — "Never" in the table at line 389. The token is displayed and copied to the clipboard as a plain URL (workspace-settings.tsx:225). Anyone who obtains such a URL — chat history, referrer, shoulder-surf — can join, and with an owner-role invite becomes a full owner able to delete the workspace. The role list and the reuse semantics look deliberate (the code comments call idempotent accept intentional), so this is hardening rather than a defect, and I could not confirm any path that leaks a token to a non-owner.

verdict.reason: Verified directly in the repository. workspace.service.ts:133-140 performs `assertOwner(workspaceId, userId)` and then `prisma.workspaceInvite.delete({ where: { id: inviteId } })` with no workspaceId in the where clause, so the authorization check is evaluated against a workspace unrelated to the row being deleted. assertOwner (workspace.service.ts:208-219) only checks WorkspaceMember role for the path workspace and never loads the invite or compares invite.workspaceId. workspace.controller.ts:103-115 resolves only the workspace slug/id and forwards the raw :inviteId path param; JwtAuthGuard (workspace.controller.ts:22) authenticates but does not tenant-scope. schema.prisma:125-136 shows WorkspaceInvite.id is a standalone @id uuid with no composite (workspaceId, id) unique, so delete-by-id matches rows in any tenant. revokeInvite has exactly one caller, so no upstream guard makes it unreachable. The codebase's own intended pattern confirms the gap: api-key.service.ts:58-63 scopes with `where: { id, workspaceId }` (fed by api-key.controller.ts:61-63) and findInvites (workspace.service.ts:126-131) scopes by workspaceId. This is an access-control/IDOR issue in the Security lane: an owner of workspace A can issue DELETE /workspaces/<A>/invites/<invite-id-of-B> and destroy another tenant's pending invite. Exploitability is bounded by needing the target invite UUID, but unguessability is not an authorization boundary, and severity is judged by impact if real, so the missing tenant scope on a destructive cross-tenant write remains blocking. No refutation ground (not-present / already-guarded / out-of-scope) applies.
